commenti.body: Not a fan of Godard (always found him pretentious and so self consciously cool) but just enjoyed Vivre Sa Vie (Live Your Life) from 1962. Not sure I would have felt the same without Anna Karina. Wow - my first experience of her. Talk about charisma. Shame the ending was such a cliché. Maybe it wasn't in 1962.
Honestly, I'm not a fan either but honestly I think that's at least partially a case of Godard the self-important public intellectual bleeding into Godard the filmmaker for me.

I walked out of Maestro. I really don’t want to go back to cinema to finish it. I’m a lifer classical musician, knew two of his mistresses, not to mention people with awful Bernstein stories. They give no life to the gay men he slept with. No depth, no character. They’re just there almost as props. “Here’s a gay guy, anyway, back to classical music and Felicia.” The gay lovers at the beginning of this film aren’t depicted as anything more than a prop. Even if the director was trying to make a scathing commentary on how Bernstein just used men in his life for sex and threw them away like Kleenex, it makes the viewer have so many more questions. Why does that man not have a real fully formed character? Why should I pull for a sex pest? The beauty of a Brokeback Mountain, a Bound, Carol, is that they respect gay characters and give them life! Maestro uses gay guys as if they were a fork, or a pack of ketchup.

Is there any way to go into Napoleon after all of these bad reviews? Ridley Scott has apparently created a #woke reimagining of Napoleon, where he’s a cuck school shooter type with mental illness. That’s so 5 years ago. I actually respected Bad Romance: The Vicky White Story because it’s a topic people don’t discuss enough. People hate incels. I don’t want to go watch a movie about an incel. Napoleon seems to have a dated theme, and with all of the talk of stealing from the Kubrick outline, do any of you think it’s worth it?

I'm relatively new to Letterboxd and "true film" in general, so I apologize if this is a dumb question.

What exactly does "kino" mean, and where did the word come from?

It's a meme that came from the /tv/ part of 4chan. It's similar to the pleb/patrician dichotomy of /mu/ where things that are 'kino' are stated as being better/more difficult/more artistic than things that are *not* 'kino'. It's a meaningless buzzword that's used in an arbitrary way.
I recognise your username from the Bernstein post before. I think you were predisposed to not like the movie. I don't know why you went to see it tbh.

The other commenter's answer isn't totally right. "Kino" is not meaningless - it is the German and Slavic word for "film." The reason it became a meme is because the (joke) sentiment is that particularly high-quality films transcend the word "movie" or "film" and should be called the foreign term "kino." It's like how people joke that there's a difference between low-brow "movies" and "intelligent" "films," just taken one step further.
Gotcha, thanks for the extra context! So is it used more tongue-in-cheek?

It is the German word for cinema, not for film and Kino has a more restrictive use than cinema in English or French, it really refers to the venue and not the films playing there. It's a clipping from Kinematograph which derives from the French cinematograph which is a device to record (graph) motion (kinema), ergo a camera. Multiple other European languages loan the word Kino from German.

Also the more highbrow German word for cinema is "Lichtspielhaus". Noone really uses it anymore but it's an amazing word.
